title: Predictive genetic testing counselling for an at-risk relative

header.contentArea: Pre-test counselling for predictive genetic testing
guidelineVersions: NICE CG164: Familial breast cancer (Published June 2013; last updated November 2023)
GMC: Decision making and consent (In effect 9 November 2020; updated 13 December 2024 and 3 August 2026)

related.why: The conversation where her mother first considered telling her
The original familial result this predictive test relates to

brief.role: Trainee supporting the genetics counselling team
brief.scenario: Freya, 20, is the daughter of a patient with a known BRCA2 pathogenic variant. She has come for pre-test counselling before deciding whether to have predictive genetic testing herself.
brief.task: Counsel her about predictive testing so she can make an informed decision. You have 7 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: This is about supporting her decision, not persuading her either way; explore her reasons for coming and what she already understands before explaining the test itself.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Assuming she has already decided to test just because she booked the appointment, and moving straight to practicalities.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Before we talk about the test itself, can I ask what's brought you here today, and what you already understand?"

flow: Explore her reasons for attending and current understanding
Explain what predictive testing can and cannot tell her
Discuss possible outcomes and their implications
Explore how she might feel about each possible result
Confirm no pressure to decide today and closing

grid.label: Exploring her starting point
grid.fail: Assumes she has already decided to test and moves straight to logistics.
grid.pass: Asks what has brought her here and what she already understands before explaining further.
grid.high: Explores whether this is her own decision or one influenced by family pressure, without being intrusive.

grid.label: Explaining the test
grid.fail: Cannot explain what predictive testing involves or what it can tell her.
grid.pass: Explains that this is a specific test for the known familial variant, and that it can tell her whether she has inherited it or not.
grid.high: Clarifies a negative result means she hasn't inherited this variant, though her general population risk for other causes remains, avoiding false reassurance.

grid.label: Explaining implications of each result
grid.fail: Only discusses one possible result (e.g. only what happens if positive).
grid.pass: Explains the implications of both a positive result (increased future risk, options for surveillance or risk-reducing measures) and a negative result.
grid.high: Explains a positive result now would mean starting surveillance discussions, while any risk-reducing surgery decisions wait until much later in life.

grid.label: Exploring emotional readiness
grid.fail: Does not explore how she thinks she would feel about either result.
grid.pass: Asks how she thinks she would feel about a positive or negative result, and what support she has around her.
grid.high: Explores this without assuming a young person's response should be uniform, allowing for however she genuinely feels.

grid.label: Insurance and practical implications
grid.fail: Does not mention any practical implications of testing, such as insurance.
grid.pass: Mentions that, under the Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance, insurers generally cannot require disclosure of a predictive genetic test result, so this is unlikely to affect standard insurance applications.
grid.high: Explains this reassuringly: insurers generally can't require predictive results, with a narrow exception only for Huntington's disease above high sums assured.

grid.label: Voluntariness and closing
grid.fail: Implies she must decide about testing today.
grid.pass: Confirms there is no pressure to decide today and that she can take as long as she needs.
grid.high: Offers a further appointment or written information, and confirms she knows how to get back in touch when and if she's ready.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: So you're here for your BRCA2 test, let's get the blood taken.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: I'm actually not sure I want to go ahead yet.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Oh. Well, it's a simple blood test either way.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Before we talk about the test itself, can I ask what's brought you here today, and what you already understand?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: My mum is BRCA2 positive, and I want to know if I have it too.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This test looks specifically for the same gene change found in your mum, so it will tell us whether you've inherited it or not.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: If it's positive, that means an increased future cancer risk, and we'd talk about surveillance options; if it's negative, you haven't inherited this particular variant.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: How do you think you'd feel with either result, and do you have support around you?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: I think I'd cope either way, my partner knows I'm here.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It's also worth knowing a genetic result can affect things like life insurance applications, which is something to factor into your decision.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: There's no pressure to decide today - take whatever time you need, and get back in touch when you're ready.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Before we talk about the test, can I ask what's brought you here, and whether this feels like your own decision or one shaped by others around you too?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: It's my decision - my mum's been really careful not to push me either way.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's good to hear. This test looks specifically for your mum's known gene change, so a positive result means you've inherited it, and a negative result means you haven't - though it's worth knowing that a negative result doesn't remove all cancer risk, just this particular inherited cause.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: What would happen if it's positive?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: At your age, that would mean starting a surveillance conversation now, like earlier or more frequent breast checks, while decisions about anything like risk-reducing surgery would be much further down the line, not something needed immediately.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: How do you think you'd feel with either result, and who do you have around you for support, whatever the outcome?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I think I'd be okay, but I'd want to know either way rather than not knowing.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's a completely valid reason to test. One practical thing worth knowing - a genetic result, whatever it shows, can be relevant to things like life insurance applications in future, so it's worth factoring that into your decision too.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: There's absolutely no pressure to decide today. I can give you written information to take away, and you can contact us whenever, if or when you're ready.

failures.move: Assuming she has already decided to test just because she attended the appointment.
failures.consequence: Removes the space for genuine informed decision-making, which pre-test counselling exists to protect.
Leaves her without a full picture to weigh her decision against, particularly the reassurance a negative result could offer.

failures.move: Omitting practical implications such as insurance.
failures.consequence: Denies her a relevant practical factor that could reasonably affect her decision or its timing.

failures.move: Cannot explain what predictive testing actually involves.
failures.consequence: Leaves her unable to weigh up whether to proceed with a test she doesn't understand.

failures.move: Implies she must decide about testing today.
failures.consequence: Pressures a decision that should be entirely voluntary and unhurried.

recovery.when: You assumed she had already decided to test
recovery.line: Let me step back - this is very much your decision, so tell me where you're at with it.

recovery.when: You only discussed a positive result
recovery.line: I should also explain what a negative result would mean for you.

knowledge.fact: Predictive genetic testing for a known familial variant tells the individual whether they have inherited that specific variant, but a negative result does not eliminate all cancer risk from other causes.
Pre-test genetic counselling should explore the individual's understanding, motivations, emotional readiness and support, without pressure to proceed.

Under the Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance (ABI/UK Government), insurers generally cannot require or request disclosure of predictive genetic test results; the only exception is Huntington's disease for life insurance above a defined sum assured. This protection can be mentioned reassuringly during pre-test counselling.

recall.think: This is her decision, not a formality; explain both possible results; mention practical implications; no pressure to decide today.
do: Explore her own reasons and understanding before explaining the test
Explain both positive and negative result implications, including practical effects like insurance
Confirm she can take as much time as she needs

numbers.meaning: chance a first-degree relative (such as a daughter) carries the same familial BRCA2 variant

recall.trap: Assuming attendance at the appointment means she has already decided to proceed with testing.
recall.finish: An informed, unpressured decision point, with written information and no obligation to decide today.

partner.opening: Please provide pre-test genetic counselling for this patient considering predictive testing. You have 7 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Freya, 20, daughter of a BRCA2-positive mother. This is genuinely your own decision, uninfluenced by family pressure, though you're anxious about what a positive result might mean for your future.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about your reasons and understanding
reveals.finding: You explain you want to know either way rather than live with uncertainty.
You feel reassured to understand what a negative result would and wouldn't mean.

reveals.trigger: Candidate confirms no pressure to decide today
reveals.finding: You feel relieved rather than rushed.

push.question: If it's positive, will I need surgery straight away?
push.expect: Clarify that at her age, surveillance would be discussed first, with surgical decisions being for much later.

push.question: Could this affect my ability to get life insurance?
push.expect: Confirm this is a genuine practical consideration worth factoring into her decision.

curveballs.prompt: My mum really wants me to test, but I'm not sure I'm ready.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Affirm that this must be her own decision regardless of her mother's wishes, and that there's no obligation to test on any particular timeline.

curveballs.prompt: What if I test negative but still get breast cancer one day?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Clarify that a negative result only rules out this specific inherited cause, not all future risk of breast cancer, and that general population screening would still apply to her.
